a: their enemies were thrown into turmoil by foul, gory blood
t: Who was troubled: the Egyptians or the river?
p: In Vaticanus the Egyptians are thrown into turmoil. Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus make the river the thing stirred up.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.plain: their enemies were thrown into turmoil by foul, gory blood

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("a perpetual running river troubled with foul blood")
readings.plain: stirred up by foul, gory blood

why: Swete's text has a masculine plural participle, which can only describe people: the Egyptians, the "enemies" of 11:5, troubled by the bloody river while Israel drank (11:7). Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have the genitive singular, which agrees with "river", and the KJV follows that sense. The plural is the harder construction, since the sentence names no subject, and a copyist could easily make the participle agree with the nearest noun. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text and supplies "their enemies" from 11:5.

p: Alexandrinus says "that we may believe in you", turning the end of the verse into the speaker's own hope.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a); the KJV ("that leaving their wickedness they may believe on thee")
readings.en: that they may believe in you, Lord
readings.plain: and believe in you, Lord

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: and we may believe in you, Lord

why: The sentence is about those God corrects ("they"), so the third person fits; Alexandrinus's "we" is one letter different in Greek and brings in the speaker's people. The first hand of Sinaiticus leaves the verb out, and a corrector added it. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text.

a: initiates from the midst of a cult band
p: Swete prints the reading of corrected Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus here; Vaticanus is garbled, and a reviser wrote "from defilement".

readings.w: Swete's text, from Codex Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a) and Codex Alexandrinus (A, which spells θειασου)
readings.en: initiates from the midst of a cult band
readings.plain: initiates from the midst of a cult band

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, a later reviser (Bᵃ), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: initiates out of the filth of a cult band

why: Swete's apparatus shows that Codex Vaticanus first wrote the letters as μυστα θειασου, which make no clear sense, and that a reviser offered both ἐκ μύσου ("from defilement") and, in the margin, a reading with "your" (σου). Swete printed the reading of corrected Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, a thiasos being a band of worshipers in a Greek cult, which makes good sense. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. The whole of 12:3–6 is a single long, rough sentence in Greek, and every translation smooths it. The first hand of Sinaiticus (ℵ*) and Codex Ephraemi (C) read μυστα θιασου, without the final letter of "initiates", much as Vaticanus first wrote it; C also has εμμεσω for "from the midst" (Swete's apparatus).

a: the arrogance of those who know it
t: Those who know, or who do not know?
p: Alexandrinus says God rebukes the arrogance of those who do not know his power; Sinaiticus says "who know you".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the KJV ("among them that know it")
readings.en: among those who know, the boldness
readings.plain: the arrogance of those who know it

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: among those who do not know
readings.plain: the arrogance of those who do not know it

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (ℵ*), from Swete's apparatus (a corrector wrote "know your")
readings.plain: the arrogance of those who know you

why: Vaticanus gives the harder thought: God shames people who know his power and still act boldly against him. Alexandrinus makes the verse a simple contrast with the first line (people who doubt, people who do not know). Sinaiticus makes "you" the object. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, which the KJV also reads.

p: The first hand of Sinaiticus leaves out "must", so the verse states what the righteous are rather than what they ought to be.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a)
readings.en: the righteous must be a lover of people
readings.plain: must love people

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (ℵ*), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: the righteous is a lover of people
readings.plain: loves people

why: Without "must" (δεῖ) the Greek still makes sense as a statement, but the corrector of Sinaiticus restored the word, and the other codices have it. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text: God's patience with enemies is a lesson that obliges his people.

a: with so much attention and entreaty
p: Vaticanus says God punished with care "and entreaty"; Sinaiticus has a rarer word; Alexandrinus and the KJV have neither.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.plain: with so much attention and entreaty

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: and diesis (a rare word from a verb meaning "let go through")
readings.plain: with so much attention and allowance

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("with such deliberation")
readings.plain: with so much attention

why: Vaticanus's "entreaty" (deēsis, usually "prayer, pleading") is odd of God punishing his enemies, unless it means that God pleaded with them by sending warnings (12:2). That oddness is probably why the other codices differ: Sinaiticus has diesis, a word built on a verb for letting something pass through, and Alexandrinus leaves the word out, as the KJV does. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text and keeps its difficulty.

t: Source of beauty or of the world?
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus wrote "the Source of the world" for "the Source of beauty".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with A and the first hand of ℵ; the KJV ("the first author of beauty")
readings.plain: the very Source of beauty

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, a corrector (ℵc.a), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: the very Source of the world

why: The verse is about beauty from start to finish ("the beauty of these things"), so "Source of beauty" fits the argument; the corrector's "world" is a later, more general reading. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text with most witnesses.

a: carves it with care when he has nothing else to do
t: In his idleness, or in his work?
p: Vaticanus says he carves in his idle hours; corrected Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say "with the care of his work".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the KJV ("when he had nothing else to do")
readings.en: in the care of his idleness
readings.plain: carves it with care when he has nothing else to do

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, a corrector (ℵc.a), and Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: in the care of his work
readings.plain: carves it with the care of his trade

why: The two words differ by a few letters (argias, ergasias). Vaticanus gives the sharper satire, that the god is made in spare time, and it matches "the skill of his free hours" later in the verse. The Plain English Translation follows Swete and the KJV.

a: the skill of his free hours
t: Skill of leisure, or of understanding?
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus wrote "understanding" for "leisure". The KJV follows the corrector.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with A
readings.plain: the skill of his free hours

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, a corrector (ℵc.a), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("by the skill of his understanding")
readings.plain: the skill of his understanding

why: Here too the words differ by a few letters (aneseōs, syneseōs). "Leisure" pairs with "idleness" earlier in the verse, the writer's point that the god is a hobby. The KJV's English follows the other reading. The Plain English Translation follows Swete.

p: Alexandrinus says the idol is more rotten than "the wood that carries him", sharpening the play on wood.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with ℵ; the KJV ("the vessel that carrieth him")
readings.plain: the ship carrying him

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: the wood carrying him

why: Alexandrinus repeats xylon, "wood", which suits the verse's wordplay so well that a copyist may have written it under the influence of the "wood" just before. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text.

p: Sinaiticus (first hand) and Alexandrinus say that "death" came into the world through human vanity, echoing 2:24.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; a corrector of Sinaiticus removed the word; the KJV ("they entered into the world")
readings.plain: They came into the world

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (ℵ*), and Codex Alexandrinus (A), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: Death came into the world

why: The subject of the Greek verb is not stated; in context it is the idols (14:13). Two codices supply "death", making the verse echo 2:24, where death entered the world through the devil's envy, and Romans 5:12. That echo is probably why the word was added; a corrector of Sinaiticus marked it for removal. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text.

p: The first hand of Sinaiticus reads "knowing your judgment" instead of "knowing your might".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a); the KJV ("knowing thy power")
readings.plain: your might

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (ℵ*), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: your judgment

why: The two words look alike in Greek (kratos, krima). "Might" matches 15:3, "knowing your might is the root from which immortality grows", and a corrector of Sinaiticus restored it. The first hand's "judgment" would make the line a confession that Israel knows God judges sin. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text.

p: Vaticanus says the sight of idols leads fools into disgrace. Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi say it stirs desire; the KJV follows them.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text
readings.plain: leads fools into disgrace

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("enticeth fools to lust after it")
readings.plain: stirs up desire in fools

why: The other three codices read oreksin, "desire", which leads naturally into the next line, "they long for", and the KJV follows it. Vaticanus's oneidos, "reproach, disgrace", also makes sense: idols bring shame on those who look on them with longing. The words look alike in capital letters. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, the base of this site; the "desire" reading has the other three great codices.

p: Alexandrinus and Ephraemi say "the one who made him". Swete's "shaped" is the verb of Genesis 2:7 in Greek.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text, with Sinaiticus
readings.plain: the one who shaped him

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: the one who made him

why: "Shaped" (plassō) is the potter's word, used of the potter in 15:7–9 and of God in the Greek of Genesis 2:7, so it carries the verse's point: the potter shapes clay but forgets the one who shaped him. "Made" (poieō) is the more common verb and is the likelier change. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text.

a: Instead he thought our life was a game
p: Vaticanus has the singular; a reviser of Vaticanus, Sinaiticus (first hand), Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and the KJV have "they".

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, first hand (B*), Swete's text, with a corrector of Sinaiticus
readings.plain: Instead he thought our life was a game

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, a reviser (Bᵃᵇ), Codex Sinaiticus first hand (ℵ*), Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus; the KJV ("they counted our life a pastime")
readings.plain: Instead they thought our life was a game

why: The potter is singular in 15:7–13, and the verb "he says" later in the verse is singular in Swete, so the singular fits. A and C also read "they say" (φασιν). The plural turns the verse into a general charge against idol-makers. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text.

a: But all the enemies of your people who oppressed them are utterly foolish
t: "All" are foolish, or the most foolish "of all"?
p: Swete's text says all of Israel's oppressors are utterly foolish. Alexandrinus and Ephraemi make them the most foolish of all.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B), Swete's text; the KJV ("And all the enemies of thy people ... are most foolish")
readings.plain: But all the enemies of your people who oppressed them are utterly foolish

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A) and Codex Ephraemi (C), from Swete's apparatus
readings.plain: But the enemies of your people who oppressed them are the most foolish of all

why: The words differ by two letters (pantes, pantōn). With "of all" the verse ranks Egypt below every other idolater, which suits 15:15, where they worship all the idols of the nations. Swete's "all" says the same of every one of Israel's oppressors. The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text, as the KJV does.
